# Part A — Creating Data Frames
## Question #1
### a. Create a vector
```{r}
student_scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)
student_scores
```

### b. Sort the scores in ascending and descending order
```{r}
# Ascending order
sort(student_scores)

# Descending order
sort(student_scores, decreasing = TRUE)
```

### c. Check if the names stayed attached to their correct values
```{r}
sorted_asc <- sort(student_scores)
sorted_asc

# Yes, the name attributes were preserved after sorting (e.g., Eli = 67, Dex = 92). 
# Since names are bound to their respective elements, sorting the vector maintains these correct pairings.
```

### d. Create another vectors
```{r}
subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)

subjects
incomplete
```

### e. Sort subjects alphabetically
```{r}
sort(subjects)
```

### f. Sort incomplete using sort()
```{r}
# By default, sort() leaves out the NA values
sort(incomplete)
# Using na.last = TRUE keeps the NAs and puts them at the end
sort(incomplete, na.last = TRUE)

# Observation: the default call quietly drops both NA values and does not show
# any warning. When na.last = TRUE is used, the NAs are kept at the end.
```

## Question #2

```{r}
# Yes, names stayed attached to their scores because they are intrinsic to the vector[cite: 2]. 
# Maintaining this binding prevents data mismatching, ensuring top scores and rankings point to the correct individuals[cite: 2].
```

```{r}
# This default behavior is risky because sort() silently removes missing (NA) valueswithout triggering a warning or an error. If I report "the lowest score" 
# without accounting for these NAs beforehand, the results will only reflect students 
# with recorded scores, creating a false impression that the dataset is complete.
```

## Question #4
### a. order() compared to sort()
```{r}
order(student_scores)
sort(student_scores)
# order() gives the positions (index numbers) of the values when they are
# arranged from smallest to largest, while sort() gives the sorted values
# themselves. So order() shows where the values are, and sort() shows what they are.
```

### b. Use order() to index student_scores
```{r}
student_scores[order(student_scores)]
sort(student_scores)
identical(student_scores[order(student_scores)], sort(student_scores))
# Yes, both give the same result. The positions from order() arrange the scores
# from smallest to largest, so using them to index student_scores does the same
# job as sort(). identical() returns TRUE, which proves it.
```

## Question #5
### a. Create a data frame
```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio")
score <- c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74)
section <- c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")
students <- data.frame(name, score, section)
students
```

### b. Reorder the ENTIRE students data frame by score
```{r}
students[order(students$score), ]
```

### c. Reorder students by score in DESCENDING order
```{r}
students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

## Question #6
```{r}
order(student_scores)
# order(student_scores) returns index numbers, such as 5 7 1 3 6 2 4, which show
# the positions of the scores from smallest to largest instead of the scores.
# Alone, it is not very useful because it does not show the actual values. It
# becomes useful when it is used to index the vector, as in
# student_scores[order(student_scores)], which rearranges the real scores.
```

## Question #7
```{r, error=TRUE}
sort(student_scores)   # works, because it is a single vector
sort(students)         # error, because it is a table with several columns

# sort() works only on a single vector, so sort(students) gives an error since a
# data frame has several columns and there is no clear way to sort all of them
# at once. order() is the right tool because students[order(students$score), ]
# moves whole rows, so the name, score, and section of each row stay together.
```

## Question #8 (rank)
### a. Use rank() and print the result
```{r}
rank(student_scores)
# Print scores and ranks side by side
cbind(scores = student_scores, rank = rank(student_scores))
# Ben and Dex both got a rank of 6.5.
```

### b. Why 6.5?
```{r}
# Ben and Dex both scored 92, resulting in a tie for the 6th and 7th ordinal positions. 
# By default, rank() applies ties.method = "average", assigning each student 
# the mean of those positions: (6 + 7) / 2 = 6.5. This is equitable because 
# neither student achieved a higher score than the other.
```

## Question #8 (sales)
### a. Create a data frame and add the rank column
```{r}
sales <- data.frame(
  employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"),
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)
)
#Minus sign gives rank 1 to TOP seller
sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)
sales
```

### b. Reorder from HIGHEST to LOWEST units_sold
```{r}
sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

## Question #9
```{r}
order(-sales$units_sold)
rank(-sales$units_sold)
# Not entirely. While order() can rearrange a table, it only returns row indices 
# (e.g., 2, 3, 5, 1, 4) rather than explicit employee standings. Furthermore, 
# order() does not explicitly indicate ties; for instance, rank() assigns Sam 
# and Tin a tied value of 1.5, whereas order() simply sequences them one after another.
```
